Social Security benefits are getting a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027. But there's another eye-catching number buried in the new benefit figures: Some retirees could receive as much as $5,358 a month. At more than $64,000 a year, it's a substantial amount of retirement income. But most Americans won't qualify for anything close to that figure, making it important to understand what Social Security will actually pay you if you're hoping to boost a fixed income . Read More Here › SPONSORED The maximum Social Security benefit will reach $5,358 The Social Security Administration (SSA) announced the new benefit figures on October 14. "Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said when announcing the increase. The maximum benefit depends on when you retire. According to SSA calculations, a worker retiring at age 70 in January 2027 who earned the maximum taxable amount throughout their career could receive $5,358 a month. By comparison, SSA estimates the average retired worker will receive $2,170 a month after the 2027 COLA, or $26,040 annually. In other words, the maximum is nearly two-and-a-half times the estimated average retirement benefit. Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started. You need a long history of high earnings Simply earning $192,300 in 2027 won't qualify you for the $5,358 monthly benefit. Social Security generally calculates your retirement benefit using your 35 highest years of indexed earnings. If you have fewer than 35 years of earnings, zeros are included in the calculation. To illustrate its 2027 maximum, SSA uses a worker who earned at least the maximum amount subject to Social Security taxes every year beginning at age 22. The threshold changes annually, rising from $147,000 in 2022 to $176,100 in 2025 and $184,500 in 2026. In 2027, it will reach $192,300. Earnings above each year's taxable maximum don't increase your Social Security benefit further. Reaching the $5,358 maximum therefore requires decades of earnings at or above those annual limits, not simply a high salary near retirement. Waiting until 70 makes a big difference Your earnings history is only part of the equation. You also need to delay claiming benefits. SSA's 2027 examples show how dramatically the maximum varies by retirement age. A worker with maximum taxable earnings who claims at 62 in 2027 could receive up to $3,094 a month. The maximum rises to $4,188 for someone retiring at full retirement age and $5,358 at 70. That's a $2,264 monthly difference between the age-62 and age-70 maximums, or $27,168 over a full year. People born in 1960 or later have a full retirement age of 67. If you're in that group, Social Security generally increases your benefit by 8% for each full year you delay beyond full retirement age until 70. Delayed retirement credits stop accumulating at 70, so waiting longer won't earn you any additional credits. Learn More Here › SPONSORED Delaying isn't automatically the right choice for everyone A larger monthly check can make waiting until 70 attractive, but it also means going years without collecting benefits. Someone eligible to claim at 62 would potentially give up eight years of payments before receiving the higher age-70 amount. Ultimately, the best time to claim depends on your personal circumstances. Your health, expected longevity, savings, other retirement income, employment plans, and whether you need Social Security to cover current expenses can all affect the decision. Delaying may be easier for someone who plans to continue working or has enough retirement savings to cover expenses in their 60s. Someone who needs the income sooner may decide that claiming earlier makes more sense despite receiving a smaller monthly benefit. The $5,358 figure is therefore useful as an illustration of what's possible, rather than a target every retiree should necessarily pursue. Working longer could help your benefit Even if the $5,358 maximum is out of reach, working longer could potentially increase your own benefit. Remember that Social Security looks at your highest 35 years of earnings. If you have fewer than 35 years in your record, another year of work could replace a zero. If you already have 35 years, a higher-earning year later in your career could replace a lower-earning year used in the calculation, potentially increasing your monthly benefit. You can check your personal earnings record through your my Social Security account. Reviewing it also gives you an opportunity to spot missing or incorrect earnings that could affect your eventual payment. Your own maximum may be much lower The $5,358 figure shouldn't be confused with a standard maximum available to everyone who waits until 70. SSA notes that retirement benefits depend on your earnings history, the age you start collecting, and the year you retire. Someone who earned $70,000 or $100,000 for much of their career, for example, won't suddenly qualify for $5,358 simply by waiting until 70. The better number to focus on is your own estimated benefit. Your Social Security account provides personalized estimates based on your actual earnings record and can show how your monthly benefit changes depending on the age you choose to claim. Retirement News: Almost 80% of Americans fear a retirement age increase — here’s the real reason why Bottom line The $5,358 maximum Social Security benefit may be out of reach for most Americans, but that doesn't mean you can't take steps to increase your own income to get closer to your retirement goals . Reviewing your Social Security earnings record, understanding how additional years of work could affect your benefit, and comparing different claiming ages can help you make a more informed decision about when to retire.
